cards.why: He reads Isaac as **present and safe**, and rejects the idea that he died.
wrong_why: Ibn Ezra rejects that reading as contradicting Scripture.
That isn't Ibn Ezra's explanation.

cards.body: The Talmud has this chapter read on the **second day of Rosh Hashanah**, to recall the binding on the day of judgment (Megillah 31a), and the **shofar** recalls it every year. Many congregations read it on Rosh Hashanah; check what CBB reads.

cards.prompt: Hineni means being fully present. Where in your life right now would you like to be able to say hineni?

points: **Hineni**: here I am, said to God, Isaac and the angel.
Rashi: "your son... your only one... whom you love... Isaac."
**The two walked together** (Rashi 22:6).
The ram's horn: **the shofar remembers the binding** (Rosh Hashanah 16a).
Ibn Ezra: Isaac was there, **safe**, at the end.

lessons.title: Abraham and Sarah (5): Sarah's life and the cave of Machpelah
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 23:1, 23:2 and 23:4, Bava Metzia 87a, Bereshit Rabbah 79:7 (read on Sefaria 11/09).

cards.title: A portion called "Life"
cards.body: This Torah portion is called **Chayei Sarah**, "the life of Sarah," yet it opens with **her death** (23:1-2). Abraham comes **to mourn her and to weep for her**, then rises to find her a resting place.

cards.q: How did Abraham get the cave of Machpelah?
choices: He paid full price for it
It was a gift he accepted
He took it in a war
cards.why: Ephron offers it as a gift, but Abraham **insists on paying** 400 shekels of silver (23:16).

cards.he:
וַיִּהְיוּ חַיֵּי שָׂרָה מֵאָה שָׁנָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה וְשֶׁבַע שָׁנִים שְׁנֵי חַיֵּי שָׂרָה
וַתָּמׇת שָׂרָה בְּקִרְיַת אַרְבַּע הִוא חֶבְרוֹן בְּאֶרֶץ כְּנָעַן וַיָּבֹא אַבְרָהָם לִסְפֹּד לְשָׂרָה וְלִבְכֹּתָהּ
cards.en: Sarah’s lifetime—the span of Sarah’s life—came to one hundred and twenty-seven years. Sarah died in Kiriath-arba—now Hebron—in the land of Canaan; and Abraham proceeded to mourn for Sarah and to bewail her.
cards.en_src: The Contemporary Torah, Jewish Publication Society, 2006
cards.tl:
Vayihyu chayei Sarah mei-ah shanah v'esrim shanah v'sheva shanim sh'nei chayei Sarah
Vatamot Sarah b'kiryat arba hi chevron b'eretz k'na-an vayavo Avraham lispod l'sarah v'livkotah

cards.he: שְׁנֵי חַיֵּי שָׂרָה
cards.tl: Sh'nei chayei Sarah
cards.gloss: **Sh'nei chayei Sarah**, "the years of Sarah's life" (23:1). The verse counts 100 years, 20 years and 7 years separately. **Rashi**: "years" is repeated to show that **all her years were equally good**.

cards.title: Why here?
cards.body: Sarah's death comes right after the binding of Isaac. **Rashi** quotes a midrash: when she heard that her son had been readied as an offering and nearly sacrificed, the shock was too much, and **she died**.

cards.q: Why does Rashi say the verse repeats the word "years"?
choices: To show all her years were equally good
To show she lived longer than Abraham
cards.why: The repetition tells us **every stage of her life was good**.
wrong_why: Rashi says nothing about comparing their ages.
Rashi reads it as praise, not doubt.

cards.he:
וַיָּקׇם אַבְרָהָם מֵעַל פְּנֵי מֵתוֹ וַיְדַבֵּר אֶל־בְּנֵי־חֵת לֵאמֹר
גֵּר־וְתוֹשָׁב אָנֹכִי עִמָּכֶם תְּנוּ לִי אֲחֻזַּת־קֶבֶר עִמָּכֶם וְאֶקְבְּרָה מֵתִי מִלְּפָנָי
cards.en: Then Abraham rose from beside his dead, and spoke to the Hittites, saying, “I am a resident alien among you; sell me a burial site among you, that I may remove my dead for burial.”
cards.en_src: The Contemporary Torah, Jewish Publication Society, 2006
cards.tl:
Vayakom Avraham mei-al p'nei meito vaydabeir el b'nei cheit leimor
Geir v'toshav anochi imachem t'nu li achuzat kever imachem v'ekb'rah meiti mil'fanai

cards.he: גֵּר־וְתוֹשָׁב אָנֹכִי עִמָּכֶם
cards.tl: Geir v'toshav anochi imachem
cards.gloss: **Ger v'toshav anochi imachem**, "I am a resident alien among you" (23:4): an outsider who has settled down. **Rashi** adds a midrash: if you sell, I'm a stranger and will pay; if not, I'll claim it as a resident, **by right**.

cards.q: What do the two words ger and toshav describe?
choices: An outsider who has settled down
cards.why: **Ger**, stranger, from another land; **toshav**, resident, settled among them. Abraham is both.
wrong_why: Neither word means king or servant.
The words describe Abraham alone.

cards.he:
וְעֶפְרוֹן יֹשֵׁב בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי־חֵת וַיַּעַן עֶפְרוֹן הַחִתִּי אֶת־אַבְרָהָם בְּאׇזְנֵי בְנֵי־חֵת לְכֹל בָּאֵי שַׁעַר־עִירוֹ לֵאמֹר
לֹא־אֲדֹנִי שְׁמָעֵנִי הַשָּׂדֶה נָתַתִּי לָךְ וְהַמְּעָרָה אֲשֶׁר־בּוֹ לְךָ נְתַתִּיהָ לְעֵינֵי בְנֵי־עַמִּי נְתַתִּיהָ לָּךְ קְבֹר מֵתֶךָ
cards.en: Ephron was present among the Hittites; so Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, the assembly in his town’s gate, saying, “No, my lord, hear me: I give you the field and I give you the cave that is in it; I give it to you in the presence of my people. Bury your dead.”
cards.en_src: The Contemporary Torah, Jewish Publication Society, 2006
cards.tl:
V'efron yosheiv b'toch b'nei cheit vaya-an efron hachiti et Avraham b'oznei v'nei cheit l'chol ba-ei sha-ar iro leimor
Lo adoni sh'ma-eini hasadeh natati lach v'ham'arah asher bo l'cha n'tatiha l'einei v'nei ami n'tatiha lach k'vor meitecha

cards.title: Say little, do much
cards.body: Ephron offers the field as a **gift**, in front of everyone (23:11). Then he names a price, 400 shekels: "what is that between you and me?" (23:15). **Rabbi Elazar**: the righteous **say little and do much**, like Abraham running to his guests; the wicked **say much and don't do even a little**, like Ephron.

cards.title: Paid in full
cards.body: Abraham **weighs out the silver** in public (23:16) and buries Sarah in the cave of Machpelah (23:19). A midrash: Machpelah is one of **three places** no one can call stolen, because they were bought: the cave of Machpelah, the Temple site and Joseph's tomb.

cards.q: Why does the midrash stress that Machpelah was paid for?
choices: So no one can say it was stolen
cards.why: It's one of three places **bought outright**, so no one can claim it was taken.
wrong_why: Ephron did offer a gift; Abraham chose to pay.
Nothing in the text says Ephron was poor.

cards.prompt: Abraham mourns, and then rises to do what has to be done (23:3). What helps you move between grieving and doing? It's fine to skip this one.

points: **Chayei Sarah**, the life of Sarah, opens with her death.
Rashi: **all her years were equally good**.
**Ger v'toshav**: an outsider who has settled down.
Bava Metzia 87a: **say little, do much** (Abraham, not Ephron).
Machpelah was **paid for**, never taken (Bereshit Rabbah 79:7).

lessons.title: Abraham and Sarah (6): Rebekah at the well
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 24:14, 24:57 and 24:67, Berakhot 26b (read on Sefaria 11/09). Ten camels: Genesis 24:10.

cards.title: A test of kindness
cards.body: Abraham sends his servant to find a wife for Isaac. At a well, the servant prays for a sign: the young woman who offers water **to him and to his camels** (24:12-14).

cards.q: What sign does the servant ask God for?
choices: A woman who offers water to him and his camels
The most beautiful woman at the well
A woman who knows Abraham's name
cards.why: The sign is **kindness beyond what's asked**: water for a stranger, and for his camels too.

cards.he:
וַיֹּאמַר יְיָ אֱלֹהֵי אֲדֹנִי אַבְרָהָם הַקְרֵה־נָא לְפָנַי הַיּוֹם וַעֲשֵׂה־חֶסֶד עִם אֲדֹנִי אַבְרָהָם
הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי נִצָּב עַל־עֵין הַמָּיִם וּבְנוֹת אַנְשֵׁי הָעִיר יֹצְאֹת לִשְׁאֹב מָיִם
וְהָיָה הַנַּעֲרָ אֲשֶׁר אֹמַר אֵלֶיהָ הַטִּי־נָא כַדֵּךְ וְאֶשְׁתֶּה וְאָמְרָה שְׁתֵה וְגַם־גְּמַלֶּיךָ אַשְׁקֶה אֹתָהּ הֹכַחְתָּ לְעַבְדְּךָ לְיִצְחָק וּבָהּ אֵדַע כִּי־עָשִׂיתָ חֶסֶד עִם־אֲדֹנִי
cards.en: And he said, “O יהוה, God of my master Abraham’s [house], grant me good fortune this day, and deal graciously with my master Abraham: Here I stand by the spring as the daughters of the townspeople come out to draw water; let the maiden to whom I say, ‘Please, lower your jar that I may drink,’ and who replies, ‘Drink, and I will also water your camels’—let her be the one whom You have decreed for Your servant Isaac. Thereby shall I know that You have dealt graciously with my master.”
cards.en_src: The Contemporary Torah, Jewish Publication Society, 2006
cards.tl:
Vayomar Adonai Elohei adoni Avraham hakrei na l'fanai hayom va-asei chesed im adoni Avraham
Hinei anochi nitzav al ein hamayim uv'not anshei ha-ir yotz'ot lish'ov mayim
V'hayah hana-ara asher omar eileha hati na chadeich v'eshteh v'amrah sh'tei v'gam g'malecha ashkeh otah hochachta l'avd'cha l'yitzchak uvah eida ki asita chesed im adoni

cards.he: וַעֲשֵׂה־חֶסֶד
cards.tl: Va-asei chesed
cards.gloss: **Va'aseh chesed**, "deal graciously" (24:12). **Chesed**, loving-kindness, is this chapter's key word: the servant asks God for chesed, and looks for a woman who shows it. **Rashi**: if she is fitting, "I'll know You have shown kindness to my master."

cards.he:
וַיָּרׇץ הָעֶבֶד לִקְרָאתָהּ וַיֹּאמֶר הַגְמִיאִינִי נָא מְעַט־מַיִם מִכַּדֵּךְ
וַתֹּאמֶר שְׁתֵה אֲדֹנִי וַתְּמַהֵר וַתֹּרֶד כַּדָּהּ עַל־יָדָהּ וַתַּשְׁקֵהוּ
וַתְּכַל לְהַשְׁקֹתוֹ וַתֹּאמֶר גַּם לִגְמַלֶּיךָ אֶשְׁאָב עַד אִם־כִּלּוּ לִשְׁתֹּת
וַתְּמַהֵר וַתְּעַר כַּדָּהּ אֶל־הַשֹּׁקֶת וַתָּרׇץ עוֹד אֶל־הַבְּאֵר לִשְׁאֹב וַתִּשְׁאַב לְכׇל־גְּמַלָּיו
cards.en: The servant ran toward her and said, “Please, let me sip a little water from your jar.” “Drink, my lord,” she said, and she quickly lowered her jar upon her hand and let him drink. When she had let him drink his fill, she said, “I will also draw for your camels, until they finish drinking.” Quickly emptying her jar into the trough, she ran back to the well to draw, and she drew for all his camels.
cards.en_src: The Contemporary Torah, Jewish Publication Society, 2006
cards.tl:
Vayarotz ha-eved likratah vayomer hagmi-ini na m'at mayim mikadeich
Vatomer sh'tei adoni vat'maheir vatored kadah al yadah vatashkeihu
Vat'chal l'hashkoto vatomer gam ligmalecha esh'av ad im kilu lishtot
Vat'maheir vat'ar kadah el hashoket vatarotz od el hab'eir lish'ov vatish'av l'chol g'malav

cards.title: She ran
cards.body: Count Rebekah's verbs: she **hurries**, lowers her jar, gives him drink, empties it, **runs** back to the well, and draws for **all** his camels (24:18-20). He had ten camels (24:10). She does far more than she was asked.

cards.q: What made Rebekah the answer to the servant's prayer?
choices: She offered water to his camels too, without being asked
She asked who his master was
cards.why: His sign was **chesed beyond the request**, and she gave it, running back again and again.
wrong_why: She was family, but that wasn't the sign he prayed for.
She didn't ask; she simply helped.

cards.he:
וַיֹּאמְרוּ נִקְרָא לַנַּעֲרָ וְנִשְׁאֲלָה אֶת־פִּיהָ
וַיִּקְרְאוּ לְרִבְקָה וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֵלֶיהָ הֲתֵלְכִי עִם־הָאִישׁ הַזֶּה וַתֹּאמֶר אֵלֵךְ
cards.en: And they said, “Let us call the girl and ask for her reply.” They called Rebekah and said to her, “Will you go with this man?” And she said, “I will.”
cards.en_src: The Contemporary Torah, Jewish Publication Society, 2006
cards.tl:
Vayomru nikra lana-ara v'nish'alah et piha
Vayikr'u l'rivkah vayomru eileha hateilchi im ha-ish hazeh vatomer eileich

cards.he: אֵלֵךְ
cards.tl: Eileich
cards.gloss: **Elech**, "I will" (24:58): one word. Her family says "let us call the girl and ask her." **Rashi**: from here we learn that a woman is not married **without her own consent**.

cards.q: What does Rashi learn from "let us call the girl and ask her"?
choices: A woman is not married without her consent
A bride must travel the same day
cards.why: Asking Rebekah teaches that **her own yes** is required.
wrong_why: The verse teaches the opposite: they ask her.
The timing isn't Rashi's point.

cards.he: לָשׂוּחַ בַּשָּׂדֶה
cards.tl: Lasuach basadeh
cards.gloss: **Lasuach basadeh**, Isaac went out "walking in the field" toward evening (24:63). **Lasuach** can also mean to converse, so the Talmud reads it as **prayer**: Abraham began the morning prayer, and **Isaac began Minchah**, the afternoon prayer.

cards.q: According to Berakhot 26b, which prayer did Isaac begin?
cards.why: From "lasuach basadeh **toward evening**": Isaac's prayer is the afternoon one.
wrong_why: The Talmud credits Abraham with the morning prayer.
That isn't Isaac's; the verse says toward evening.

cards.title: Comfort after his mother
cards.body: Isaac brings Rebekah into **his mother Sarah's tent**, loves her, and is comforted after his mother (24:67). **Rashi** quotes a midrash: in Sarah's lifetime a **lamp burned** from one Shabbat eve to the next, there was **blessing in the dough** and a **cloud** over the tent. They stopped when she died, and **returned with Rebekah**.
In the Amidah's first blessing you say **Elohei Rivkah**, God of Rebekah, right after Elohei Sarah. And every **Minchah** is, in the Talmud's reading, Isaac's walk in the field.

points: The sign: **chesed beyond the request** (24:14).
Rebekah **runs** to water ten camels.
**Elech**, "I will": Rashi, no marriage **without her consent**.
**Lasuach basadeh**: Isaac begins **Minchah** (Berakhot 26b).
Sarah's lamp, dough and cloud **return with Rebekah** (Rashi 24:67).

lessons.title: Jacob and Esau (1): Twins and the birthright
lessons.check_note: My summaries of Rashi on Genesis 25:22, 25:27 and 25:30 (with Bereshit Rabbah 63 and Bava Batra 16b), read on Sefaria 11/09. Note the Contemporary Torah renders yoshev ohalim as 'raising livestock'.

cards.title: Two in one womb
cards.body: Rebekah's twins **struggle inside her** (25:22). She asks the question people in pain ask, **why?**, and then goes **to inquire of God**.

cards.q: Rebekah keeps her distress to herself.
cards.why: She speaks it aloud and **goes to inquire of Adonai** (25:22), and God answers her.

cards.he:
וַיֶּעְתַּר יִצְחָק לַיהֹוָה לְנֹכַח אִשְׁתּוֹ כִּי עֲקָרָה הִוא וַיֵּעָתֶר לוֹ יְיָ וַתַּהַר רִבְקָה אִשְׁתּוֹ
וַיִּתְרֹצְצוּ הַבָּנִים בְּקִרְבָּהּ וַתֹּאמֶר אִם־כֵּן לָמָּה זֶּה אָנֹכִי וַתֵּלֶךְ לִדְרֹשׁ אֶת־יְיָ
וַיֹּאמֶר יְיָ לָהּ שְׁנֵי גוֹיִם בְּבִטְנֵךְ וּשְׁנֵי לְאֻמִּים מִמֵּעַיִךְ יִפָּרֵדוּ וּלְאֹם מִלְאֹם יֶאֱמָץ וְרַב יַעֲבֹד צָעִיר
cards.en: Isaac pleaded with יהוה on behalf of his wife, because she was barren; and יהוה responded to his plea, and his wife Rebekah conceived. But the children struggled in her womb, and she said, “If so, why do I exist?” She went to inquire of יהוה, and יהוה answered her, “Two nations are in your womb, Two separate peoples shall issue from your body; One people shall be mightier than the other, And the older shall serve the younger.”
cards.en_src: The Contemporary Torah, Jewish Publication Society, 2006
cards.tl:
Vayetar Yitzchak laihovah l'nochach ishto ki akarah hi vayei-ater lo Adonai vatahar Rivkah ishto
Vayitrotz'tzu habanim b'kirbah vatomer im kein lamah zeh anochi vateilech lidrosh et Adonai
Vayomer Adonai lah sh'nei goyim b'vitneich ush'nei l'umim mimei-ayich yipareidu ul'om mil'om ye-ematz v'rav ya-avod tza-ir

cards.he: לָמָּה זֶּה אָנֹכִי
cards.tl: Lamah zeh anochi
cards.gloss: **Lamah zeh anochi**, "why do I exist?" or "why am I like this?" (25:22). Rebekah doesn't stop at the question: she goes **lidrosh**, to seek out God.

cards.title: Running to the doors
cards.body: **Rashi** reads "struggled" as **running**: whenever Rebekah passed a house of Torah study, **Jacob** strained to come out; whenever she passed a pagan temple, **Esau** did. He also gives the plain reading: the twins **fought** with each other.

cards.q: In Rashi's midrash, why did the twins move inside Rebekah?
choices: Each was drawn to a different kind of place
They wanted to be born first
cards.why: Jacob toward **houses of study**, Esau toward **pagan temples**: two paths from the start.
wrong_why: Hunger isn't part of this midrash.
Rashi's midrash here is about where each was drawn, not birth order.

cards.he:
וַיִּגְדְּלוּ הַנְּעָרִים וַיְהִי עֵשָׂו אִישׁ יֹדֵעַ צַיִד אִישׁ שָׂדֶה וְיַעֲקֹב אִישׁ תָּם יֹשֵׁב אֹהָלִים
וַיֶּאֱהַב יִצְחָק אֶת־עֵשָׂו כִּי־צַיִד בְּפִיו וְרִבְקָה אֹהֶבֶת אֶת־יַעֲקֹב
cards.en: When the boys grew up, Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the outdoors; but Jacob became a mild man, raising livestock. Isaac favored Esau because he had a taste for game; but Rebekah favored Jacob.
cards.en_src: The Contemporary Torah, Jewish Publication Society, 2006
cards.tl:
Vayigd'lu han'arim vay'hi eisav ish yodeia tzayid ish sadeh v'ya-akov ish tam yosheiv ohalim
Vaye-ehav Yitzchak et eisav ki tzayid b'fiv v'rivkah ohevet et Yaakov

cards.he: אִישׁ תָּם יֹשֵׁב אֹהָלִים
cards.tl: Ish tam yosheiv ohalim
cards.gloss: **Ish tam yoshev ohalim**: this translation says "a mild man, raising livestock"; word for word, "a **whole** man, **dwelling in tents**." **Rashi**: tam means his heart matched his mouth, not clever at deceiving; the tents are the study tents of **Shem and Ever**.

cards.q: What does Rashi say tam means?
cards.why: **Tam**: whole, straightforward. What was in his heart was in his mouth.
wrong_why: Tam isn't about strength.
Tam describes character, not birth order.

cards.he:
וַיָּזֶד יַעֲקֹב נָזִיד וַיָּבֹא עֵשָׂו מִן־הַשָּׂדֶה וְהוּא עָיֵף
וַיֹּאמֶר עֵשָׂו אֶל־יַעֲקֹב הַלְעִיטֵנִי נָא מִן־הָאָדֹם הָאָדֹם הַזֶּה כִּי עָיֵף אָנֹכִי עַל־כֵּן קָרָא־שְׁמוֹ אֱדוֹם
וַיֹּאמֶר יַעֲקֹב מִכְרָה כַיּוֹם אֶת־בְּכֹרָתְךָ לִי
cards.en: Once when Jacob was cooking a stew, Esau came in from the open, famished. And Esau said to Jacob, “Give me some of that red stuff to gulp down, for I am famished”—which is why he was named Edom. Jacob said, “First sell me your birthright.”
cards.en_src: The Contemporary Torah, Jewish Publication Society, 2006
cards.tl:
Vayazed Yaakov nazid vayavo eisav min hasadeh v'hu ayeif
Vayomer eisav el Yaakov hal'iteini na min ha-adom ha-adom hazeh ki ayeif anochi al kein kara sh'mo edom
Vayomer Yaakov michrah chayom et b'choratcha li

cards.title: A mourner's meal
cards.body: Why was Jacob cooking lentils? **Rashi**: **Abraham died that day**, and Jacob was preparing the first meal for the mourners. Lentils are **round like a wheel**, because mourning is a wheel that comes around to everyone.

cards.he:
וַיֹּאמֶר עֵשָׂו הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ לָמוּת וְלָמָּה־זֶּה לִי בְּכֹרָה
וַיֹּאמֶר יַעֲקֹב הִשָּׁבְעָה לִּי כַּיּוֹם וַיִּשָּׁבַע לוֹ וַיִּמְכֹּר אֶת־בְּכֹרָתוֹ לְיַעֲקֹב
וְיַעֲקֹב נָתַן לְעֵשָׂו לֶחֶם וּנְזִיד עֲדָשִׁים וַיֹּאכַל וַיֵּשְׁתְּ וַיָּקׇם וַיֵּלַךְ וַיִּבֶז עֵשָׂו אֶת־הַבְּכֹרָה
cards.en: And Esau said, “I am at the point of death, so of what use is my birthright to me?” But Jacob said, “Swear to me first.” So he swore to him, and sold his birthright to Jacob. Jacob then gave Esau bread and lentil stew; he ate and drank, and he rose and went away. Thus did Esau spurn the birthright.
cards.en_src: The Contemporary Torah, Jewish Publication Society, 2006
cards.tl:
Vayomer eisav hinei anochi holeich lamut v'lamah zeh li b'chorah
Vayomer Yaakov hishav'ah li kayom vayishava lo vayimkor et b'chorato l'ya-akov
V'ya-akov natan l'eisav lechem un'zid adashim vayochal vayeisht vayakom vayeilach vayivez eisav et hab'chorah

cards.he: וַיִּבֶז עֵשָׂו אֶת־הַבְּכֹרָה
cards.tl: Vayivez eisav et hab'chorah
cards.gloss: **Vayivez Esav et hab'chorah**, "thus did Esau spurn the birthright" (25:34). The Torah's own verdict comes after a rush of verbs: **he ate, drank, rose and went**.

cards.q: Whom does the last line of the story judge?
choices: Jacob, for driving a hard bargain
cards.why: The verse names **Esau**: he "spurned the birthright."
wrong_why: The Torah doesn't comment on Jacob here, though readers have long argued about him.
Isaac isn't in this scene.

cards.body: Jacob is the one who **dwells in tents**. Every Shabbat morning you open with **Mah tovu ohalecha Yaakov**, "how good are your tents, Jacob" (Numbers 24:5).

points: **Lamah zeh anochi**: Rebekah's why becomes a search for God.
Rashi: the twins ran toward **study houses** and **temples**.
**Ish tam**: heart and mouth matched (Rashi 25:27).
The lentils: **a mourner's meal** for Abraham (Rashi 25:30).
**Vayivez Esav**: the Torah's verdict on the sale.

units.title: Holiday stories
units.subtitle: The stories behind Shavuot, Hanukkah and Yom Kippur afternoon

lessons.title: Ruth: The stranger who stayed
lessons.check_note: My retelling of Ruth 1-4 and Leviticus 19:9-10; quotes are paraphrased. Check most closely: Ruth Rabbah 2:14 (purpose of the book) and the Shavuot traditions. Does CBB read Ruth on Shavuot?

cards.title: Three widows
cards.body: A famine drives **Elimelech and Naomi** from Bethlehem to **Moab**, an old rival nation. Their sons marry Moabite women, **Orpah and Ruth**. Then all three men die, leaving three widows with no one to support them.

cards.q: Naomi tells both daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers' homes. What does Ruth do?
choices: Asks Naomi to stay in Moab
cards.why: Ruth **refuses to leave**. Naomi's people will be her people, and Naomi's God her God.

cards.title: Where you go, I will go
cards.body: Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye. Ruth holds on. Wherever Naomi goes and wherever she sleeps, Ruth will too; **Naomi's people will be her people and Naomi's God her God**, and only death will part them.

cards.he:
וַתֹּאמֶר רוּת אַל־תִּפְגְּעִי־בִי לְעׇזְבֵךְ לָשׁוּב מֵאַחֲרָיִךְ כִּי אֶל־אֲשֶׁר תֵּלְכִי אֵלֵךְ וּבַאֲשֶׁר תָּלִינִי אָלִין עַמֵּךְ עַמִּי וֵאלֹהַיִךְ אֱלֹהָֽי׃
בַּאֲשֶׁר תָּמוּתִי אָמוּת וְשָׁם אֶקָּבֵר כֹּה יַעֲשֶׂה יְיָ לִי וְכֹה יוֹסִיף כִּי הַמָּוֶת יַפְרִיד בֵּינִי וּבֵינֵֽךְ׃
cards.en: But Ruth replied, “Do not urge me to leave you, to turn back and not follow you. For wherever you go, I will go; wherever you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. Thus and more may GOD do to me if anything but death parts me from you.”
cards.en_src: THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition
cards.tl:
Vatomer Rut al tifg'i vi l'ozveich lashuv mei-acharayich ki el asher teilchi eileich uva-asher talini alin ameich ami veilohayich Elohai.
Ba-asher tamuti amut v'sham ekaveir ko ya-aseh Adonai li v'cho yosif ki hamavet yafrid beini uveineich.

cards.title: Gleaning
cards.body: They reach Bethlehem as the **barley harvest** begins. Ruth goes out to **glean**, picking up the grain the reapers leave behind. The Torah tells farmers to leave the edges of the field and the fallen grain **for the poor and the stranger**. Ruth is both.

cards.q: Why could Ruth gather grain in a field that wasn't hers?
choices: The Torah leaves gleanings for the poor and the stranger
Naomi owned part of the field
cards.why: Leaving gleanings is a **Torah law**: the edges and the fallen grain belong to the poor and the stranger.
wrong_why: Boaz only notices her after she is already gleaning. He never hires her.
Naomi came home with nothing. She had no crop.

cards.title: Boaz
cards.body: The field belongs to **Boaz**, a relative of Elimelech. He has heard how Ruth stood by Naomi. He tells her to stay in his field, orders his workers not to bother her, and has them pull out extra stalks for her to gather.

cards.title: The redeemer
cards.body: Naomi sends Ruth to ask Boaz to be her **go'el**, redeemer: the relative who takes responsibility for a family's land and name. A closer relative turns it down and seals it by handing over his sandal. **Boaz marries Ruth.**

cards.he: כִּי גֹאֵל אָתָּה
cards.tl: Ki go-eil atah
cards.gloss: "For you are a **redeemer**" (3:9). Ruth asks Boaz to step in as **go'el**, the relative who takes responsibility for the family.

cards.q: What was a go'el, a redeemer, in Ruth's world?
choices: A relative who takes responsibility for a family's land and name
cards.why: The go'el is a **relative** who steps in for a family that has lost its men.
wrong_why: Boaz settles it at the town gate in front of elders, but as a relative, not as a judge.
No priest appears anywhere in the book.

cards.title: Great-grandmother of a king
cards.body: Their son is **Obed**, the father of Jesse, the father of **King David**. The book ends with a family tree: Israel's greatest king descends from a woman of Moab.

cards.q: Who is Ruth's great-grandson?
cards.why: Obed, then Jesse, then **David**.
wrong_why: Solomon is David's son, one generation further down.
Samuel anoints David as king but isn't related to Ruth.

cards.title: Hesed
cards.body: A midrash asks why this book was written at all, since it teaches no laws. Its answer: **to teach how great the reward is for hesed**, loyal kindness. Ruth shows it to Naomi, and Boaz to Ruth, each going beyond what was required.

cards.he: הֵיטַבְתְּ חַסְדֵּךְ הָאַחֲרוֹן מִן־הָרִאשׁוֹן
cards.tl: Heitavt chasdeich ha-acharon min harishon
cards.gloss: "Your latest **hesed** is greater than your first" (3:10). Boaz praises Ruth's loyal kindness: first to Naomi, now to the whole family.

cards.q: Put the story in order.
items: Famine and the move to Moab
cards.why: Loss, then loyalty, then kindness answered with kindness, then a royal line.

cards.body: Many congregations read Ruth on **Shavuot**. It is a harvest story for a harvest festival, and Ruth's choice to join the Jewish people is often linked to Israel accepting the Torah at Sinai. A tradition also holds that David was born and died on Shavuot.

cards.prompt: Ruth committed before she knew anything would turn out well. Where in your own Jewish life did you choose first and understand later?

points: Three widows; Ruth **won't leave Naomi**.
She **gleans**, a right the Torah gives the poor and the stranger.
Boaz acts as **go'el** and marries her.
Their great-grandson is **King David**.
The midrash: the book teaches **hesed**.

lessons.title: Hanukkah: The rededication
lessons.check_note: Dates follow the usual scholarly reconstruction from 1 Maccabees. 'Hammer' for Maccabee is the common explanation, not certain. Decide whether the app should mention the classical Reform framing (religious freedom).

cards.title: A story outside the Bible
cards.body: Hanukkah's story **isn't in the Hebrew Bible**. It comes from the **books of Maccabees**, written in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE and left out of the Jewish canon, and from the **Talmud**, centuries later.

src.note: Kept in the Septuagint and Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, not in the Tanakh.

cards.q: What did the first Hanukkah celebrate?
choices: A jar of oil lasting eight days
cards.why: The earliest source celebrates **rededicating the Temple**. The oil story appears centuries later.

cards.body: Judea is ruled by the **Seleucid** Greek kingdom. Many Jews have taken up Greek culture, and Jews argue bitterly among themselves about how far to go.
King **Antiochus IV** bans Shabbat, circumcision and Torah study, and sets up pagan worship in the **Temple in Jerusalem**.

cards.title: Mattathias says no
cards.body: In the village of **Modi'in**, an old priest named **Mattathias** refuses to sacrifice to the king's gods. He and his sons flee to the hills and start a revolt.

cards.q: What started the revolt?
choices: A priest refused to offer a pagan sacrifice
The Temple ran out of oil
cards.why: In Modi'in, **Mattathias refused** to sacrifice to the king's gods.
wrong_why: The oil story is about the end of the war, and it comes from a much later source.
1 Maccabees tells it as a fight over religion, not money.

cards.title: The hammer
cards.body: His son **Judah** leads the fighting and is nicknamed **Maccabee**, usually explained as "the hammer." Against a much larger army, the rebels win back Jerusalem.

src.note: The meaning of Maccabee is uncertain.

cards.body: They purify the Temple, build a new altar and **rededicate** it with eight days of celebration. **Hanukkah** means "dedication."

src.note: 2 Maccabees 10:6 says the eight days were kept like a late Sukkot.

cards.he: חֲנֻכַּת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ
cards.tl: Chanukat hamizbeiach
cards.gloss: "The **dedication of the altar**" (Numbers 7:84). The same word names the dedication of the Tabernacle's altar in the Torah. That chapter is the Torah reading during Hanukkah.

cards.q: What does the word Hanukkah mean?
cards.why: It names the **rededication** of the Temple and its altar.
wrong_why: Light is the holiday's symbol, but the word itself means dedication.
The victory made it possible, but the name is about the Temple.

cards.title: The jar of oil
cards.body: Centuries later the **Talmud** asks, "What is Hanukkah?" and tells a new story: one sealed jar of pure oil, enough for one day, **burned for eight**.

cards.q: Where does the story of the oil first appear?
cards.why: The Babylonian **Talmud**, Shabbat 21b.
wrong_why: 1 Maccabees has eight days of celebration but no oil miracle.
Hanukkah happened long after the Torah was written.

cards.title: Not by might
cards.body: The haftarah for Shabbat of Hanukkah answers the war story. The prophet Zechariah sees a golden lampstand and hears: **not by might and not by power, but by My spirit**.

cards.he: וַיַּעַן וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלַי לֵאמֹר זֶה דְּבַר־יְיָ אֶל־זְרֻבָּבֶל לֵאמֹר לֹא בְחַיִל וְלֹא בְכֹחַ כִּי אִם־בְּרוּחִי אָמַר יְיָ צְבָאֽוֹת׃
cards.en: Then he explained to me as follows: “This is the word of GOD to Zerubbabel: Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit—said GOD of Hosts.
cards.en_src: THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition
cards.tl: Vaya-an vayomer eilai leimor zeh d'var Adonai el Z'rubavel leimor lo v'chayil v'lo v'choach ki im b'ruchi amar Adonai tz'va-ot.

cards.q: Put the events in order.
cards.why: Persecution, refusal, revolt, victory, rededication.

cards.body: When you light the candles you hold **both stories**: a stubborn fight for the freedom to live as Jews, and a small light that lasts longer than it should. Different generations have leaned on one or the other.

cards.prompt: Which story speaks to you more right now, the fight or the light? Why?

points: The story comes from **Maccabees** and the **Talmud**, not the Bible.
Antiochus IV **banned Jewish practice**; Mattathias refused.
Judah **the Maccabee** retook Jerusalem.
Hanukkah means **dedication**: the Temple, 25 Kislev.
The **oil** story is from the Talmud; the haftarah says **not by might**.

lessons.title: Jonah: The prophet who ran
lessons.check_note: My retelling of Jonah 1-4; quotes are paraphrased. Confirm that Mishkan HaNefesh and CBB read Jonah on Yom Kippur afternoon.

cards.title: The other direction
cards.body: God tells **Jonah** to go to **Nineveh**, capital of Assyria, Israel's enemy, and call out against its evil. Jonah goes down to **Jaffa** and boards a ship sailing the opposite way, to **Tarshish**.

cards.q: Why did Jonah run, by his own account?
choices: He knew God would forgive Nineveh
He was afraid of being killed
He didn't believe God had spoken
cards.why: He says it himself near the end: he knew God was **gracious and compassionate** and would relent.

cards.title: The storm
cards.body: A great storm hits. The sailors pray, each to his own god, and **cast lots**; the lot falls on Jonah, asleep below deck. He tells them to **throw him overboard**. They try rowing to shore first, then do it, and the sea goes calm.

cards.title: The fish
cards.body: God sends a **great fish** to swallow Jonah. He is inside it for three days and three nights, and **he prays**. Then the fish spits him out onto dry land.

cards.q: How did the sailors find out the storm was about Jonah?
choices: Another prophet on board told them
cards.why: They **cast lots**, and the lot fell on Jonah.
wrong_why: He explains himself only after the lot falls on him.
There is no other prophet in the story.

cards.title: Five words
cards.body: God asks a second time, and Jonah goes. His whole message is **five words in Hebrew**: forty more days, and Nineveh will be overturned.

cards.he: וַיָּחֶל יוֹנָה לָבוֹא בָעִיר מַהֲלַךְ יוֹם אֶחָד וַיִּקְרָא וַיֹּאמַר עוֹד אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם וְנִֽינְוֵה נֶהְפָּֽכֶת׃
cards.en: Jonah started out and made his way into the city the distance of one day’s walk, and proclaimed: “Forty days more, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!”
cards.en_src: THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition
cards.license: CC-BY-NC (Sefaria lists 'unknown' for Jonah; same edition as Ruth and Zechariah)
cards.tl: Vayachel Yonah lavo va-ir mahalach yom echad vayikra vayomar od arba-im yom v'Nin'veih nehpachet.

cards.title: A city turns
cards.body: The people believe. **Everyone fasts and wears sackcloth**, from the king down, and the king orders even the **animals** to fast. They turn from violence, and God does not destroy the city.

cards.he: כִּי־שָׁבוּ מִדַּרְכָּם הָרָעָה
cards.tl: Ki shavu midarkam hara-ah
cards.gloss: "They **turned** from their evil way" (3:10). **Shavu**, they turned, comes from the same root as **teshuvah**.

cards.q: Who repents in Nineveh?
choices: Only the people who heard Jonah
cards.why: The king's decree covers **people and animals alike**.
wrong_why: The king leads, but his decree covers the whole city.
The people start it, but the king's decree spreads it to everyone, animals included.

cards.title: Jonah's anger
cards.body: Jonah is furious. This is why he ran, he says: he knew God is **gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in kindness**, and would relent. He is quoting the attributes God revealed to Moses.

cards.q: Why does Jonah's complaint sound familiar?
choices: He quotes God's attributes from Exodus 34
cards.why: He turns God's own words to Moses, **gracious and compassionate**, into a complaint.
wrong_why: The sailors' prayer asks not to be blamed for his death; it has different words.
The king hopes God may relent, but Jonah's words come from Exodus.

cards.title: The plant
cards.body: Jonah sits outside the city to see what will happen. God grows a plant to shade him, then sends a worm to kill it. In the hot sun, Jonah says he would rather die.

cards.title: The last question
cards.body: God answers: you care about a plant you didn't plant or grow. **Should I not care about Nineveh**, with more than 120,000 people who can't tell their right hand from their left, and many animals? The book ends there. **Jonah never answers.**

cards.q: Put the story in order.
cards.why: Flight, storm, prayer, warning, repentance, and a question left open.

cards.body: Jonah is read on **Yom Kippur afternoon**. On the day of teshuvah, turning, you hear about a whole city that turned, and a prophet who found God's mercy hard to accept. All day you also sing the same attributes Jonah quotes.

cards.prompt: The book ends with a question nobody answers. How would you answer in Jonah's place?

points: Jonah **runs** from his mission to Nineveh.
Storm, lots, and **three days in the fish**.
**Five words**, and the whole city repents, animals too.
Jonah is angry that God is **gracious and compassionate** (Exodus 34).
The book ends with **God's question**, unanswered.
